extracted.intended_audience: college/university instructors of undergraduate mathematics (course designers and graders)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical classroom assessment techniques and grading methods for undergraduate mathematics courses, including design and scoring of interactive quizzes (IQs), portfolio polling, flexible grade weightings, one-minute papers, concept maps, and written-homework guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: IQ part-wise scoring and help-screen penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Each IQ problem is divided into parts with point values for each part; help-screen menu items have numeric point costs shown after each item (e.g., [0.0], [1.2], [2.2], [3.3], [4.3]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students choose a help-menu item before answering; choosing nonzero help items reduces the score for that part by the indicated amount. Choosing 0.0 allows students to type written answers which are sent to the instructor. Students may retry menus any time; help use before submission is recorded and returned with the answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track and report student help usage in IQs
rubrics_metrics.description: The IQ system tracks which help screens a student used and returns that data to the instructor via e-mail and places it in the student's portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor receives both the written answers and any help usage; this helps diagnose misunderstandings and shows what students would have gained by using certain help screens (example: Akoines vs Gmoore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tagging of IQ pieces for automated portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of each problem in an IQ has a tag to simplify moving student responses into portfolios and gathering responses to a given question across students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tags allow assembling all students' answers to the same item (as if ripping bluebooks apart) for batch grading, reporting, and focused instructor feedback. Proper tagging is required to enable easy polling and batch operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polling portfolios (aggregate reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polling portfolios means collecting IQ and other interaction data from student portfolios to create instantaneous reports about how a collection of students answered a specific question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By default only the instructor has access to the portfolio. The polling feature supports creating reports across students and across time to detect persistent misconceptions and forgetting (e.g., recurring errors weeks later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Batch evaluating and commenting on portfolio pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewer programs permit batching evaluation/commenting on specific IQ pieces and sending a single response to many students' portfolios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor can write one response once and tag which students should receive it; this speeds grading and feedback (example: sending the same corrective reply to many students who made the same error). The system can also mail commented IQ portions to portfolio owners automatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TeX for precise mathematical e-mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Running e-mail exchanges through a TeX compiler promotes precision in mathematical writing and translates symbols to high-quality output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce TeX incrementally so students adopt precise notation; compiled output is a pedagogical reward and facilitates clearer mathematical exposition in portfolios and email.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design IQ help screens from minimal hints to fuller steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Help screens should be offered at multiple levels (e.g., choosing an example, checking a computation, describing the set, solving equations) with increasing point cost for more revealing help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label help options clearly and assign point penalties that reflect their helpfulness; include a 'No help needed' option. Help-level granularity lets students get scaffolding without immediately receiving full solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow retrying IQs after instructor return
rubrics_metrics.description: After returning the IQ to the instructor, a student can go through it again, this time optionally using the help screens to check work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports iterative learning: initial attempt (graded with help-penalties) followed by remedial use of help for learning rather than grade improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use portfolios to detect learning decay over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting and polling past IQs and portfolio artifacts makes visible when students have forgotten material introduced weeks earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create reports from earlier IQs to show students recurring misunderstandings and motivate study habit changes; use polling to find problems that reoccur and address them promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible grade weighting (student-selected weights within instructor-defined ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students choose what percent (within instructor-set ranges) of their grade comes from each required activity, allowing them to emphasize strengths and de-emphasize weak areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor distributes a form listing ranges for each factor early in course; students choose weights (often after the first exam/project), sign the form, and cannot change choices later. Typical categories and example ranges are provided (e.g., homework 30–45%, hour exams 15–25%, final 20–40%, projects 5–20%, journal 10–30%, board presentations 5–10%, self-evaluation 5%, teacher-evaluation 5%). Spreadsheets or calculator programs can auto-compute final grades from chosen weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set minimum/maximum bounds and combined constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor must set bounds so certain components maintain sufficient influence (e.g., quizzes and final combined minimum of 45%), implicitly constraining how much weight students can allocate elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bounds preserve course priorities (e.g., ensure exams matter) while allowing student choice. To prevent some activities from being optional, set their lower bound above zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include small mandatory minima to encourage engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Give small nonzero lower bounds (e.g., 5%) for categories like journal, board presentations, self-evaluation, and teacher-evaluation instead of allowing zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small cost (5%) signals that all assessment methods are important and motivates participation (example: fearful students still present to avoid losing five points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-evaluation and teacher-evaluation as grade components
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a self-evaluation (e.g., 5%) where students justify their grade and a teacher-evaluation (e.g., 5%) where instructor records significant observations about effort and contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-evaluations should be assessed for quality; poor justification yields low score on that component. Teacher-evaluation requires systematic record-keeping of participation, contributions, lapses; if no negatives recorded, student receives full points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative requirements for flexible weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must sign and submit a form listing their chosen weights; instructor records final numerical grade on that form; choices are final after submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spreadsheets or calculator programs to automate grade calculation. Discuss ranges early in course and allow students time to experience the class before selecting weights (often shortly after first exam/project).

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage thoughtful portfolio/journal writing with grading incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Require brief expository work such as journals or self-evaluations and use grading to improve the depth of student reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduct points for shallow expository responses; provide targeted follow-up questions when reflections are superficial; place some small minimum weight to motivate consistent effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-minute paper: two focused end-of-class prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask students in the last minute (or three) of class to write short answers to: (1) What was the most important point made in class today? and (2) What unanswered question do you still have?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 3×5 cards or students' paper; allow anonymity to encourage candidness or require names to permit personalized replies; give small participation credit to encourage regular completion. Instructor can write one-sentence responses and return them. Variations include asking students to name five significant points.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-minute paper: use and follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Use collected responses to identify common confusions and start the next class by addressing misunderstandings or building on students' questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In large classes keep the exercise brief (instructor can spend <30 minutes responding to a batch); consistency and early discussion of expectations improves the quality of student responses. Refining the prompt (e.g., ask for 'most surprising moment') helps avoid vague answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-minute paper success factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To be effective the technique must be regular, consistent, and accompanied by early instruction on what constitutes a useful response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend class time modeling specific observations and question formulation; offer small bonus credit for consistently good questions; adjust prompts to elicit concrete observations rather than generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept maps for formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use concept maps (diagrams showing connections between major concepts) to reveal students' structural knowledge and prerequisite concept gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a schematic and a collection of terms for students to place in ovals and link; allow text/reference and small-group discussion but avoid giving too many prompts. Walk around to monitor errors and questions; use maps to diagnose misconceptions and determine needed review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept map variants and classroom practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative approaches include asking students to create maps without a preset schematic, gathering and discussing those maps, or brainstorming related concepts then labeling relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and critique student-generated maps publicly to highlight missing relations or good features; be cautious about moving to group work too quickly; use maps especially when dealing with related or subclass concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for written homework (expository requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require an expository paragraph describing how students arrived at solutions, how the problem relates to class, what they learned, what they tried if unsuccessful, and what obstacles remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly tell students 'The most important thing is to demonstrate ... that some thought went into your work.' Use grading power to enforce depth: deduct points for missing or shallow expository sections and include probing questions to encourage deeper reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use homework expository responses diagnostically
rubrics_metrics.description: Read students' expository reflections to understand their thought evolution, whether they learned new mathematics, and whether they can distinguish example-based reasoning from general justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use students' reflective comments to guide personal feedback, to identify students who have improved conceptual understanding despite not fully solving problems, and to adapt subsequent instruction (examples: students recognizing 'division' vs 'cancellation' issues in abstract algebra).
